Saudi condemns ‘terrorist attack’ after Riyadh skyscraper hit twice in a week

An attack on the PIF tower is symbolic as it houses the Saudi sovereign wealth fund driving efforts to diversify the oil-reliant economy

Agence France-Presse
Published: 11:35pm, 24 Nov 2026Updated: 2:28am, 25 Nov 2026
The tallest skyscraper in Saudi Arabia’s capital of Riyadh was struck for the second time in days on Tuesday, witnesses said, as the coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis denounced a “terrorist attack”.

Three separate witnesses said the strike targeted the 80-storey Public Investment Fund (PIF) Tower, which houses the kingdom’s sovereign wealth fund and dominates Riyadh’s King Abdullah Financial District (KAFD).

The building, which was also attacked on Thursday, is one of several high-profile targets hit since hostilities with the Iran-backed Houthis restarted in July.

“One of the towers in the financial centre was targeted in a cowardly terrorist attack,” coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said in a social media post, without naming the building. “The relevant authorities are currently inspecting the attack site.”

An attack on the PIF is symbolic as the fund is driving efforts to diversify the oil-reliant Saudi economy – a project that has been complicated by the Middle East war and Houthi strikes.

A tower belonging to state oil giant Aramco in KAFD was hit earlier this month, while Riyadh’s international airport was repeatedly struck in October with one attack killing 14 people.
A screengrab from a social media video shows a projectile hitting the Public Investment Fund Tower on Thursday. Photo: Reuters

A fourth witness said a vehicle fitted with a speaker had warned pedestrians in the area to take cover on Tuesday. No warning was sent to mobile phones about any threats to the capital.

Afterwards, police cars blocked some entrances to the gleaming financial district, a showpiece of Saudi Arabia’s modernisation under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the de facto ruler.

“We just reopened a while ago,” a waiter at a KAFD restaurant said. “They evacuated all of us telling us a tower has been hit. They closed the streets and they banned people from passing in streets or entering.”

Last week, Saudi officials said an attack on a tower in the financial district damaged several floors and two adjacent buildings but caused no casualties.

Although authorities did not identify the building, photos released by the civil defence agency appeared to show shattered glass and other exterior damage to the PIF tower.

The Houthis claimed responsibility for last week’s attack, but they did not announce any fresh attacks on Tuesday.

Standing 385 metres (1,300 feet) high, the PIF tower is the most prominent landmark of KAFD, a showcase for Saudi Arabia’s economic ambitions.

With imposing skyscrapers, luxury shops and green spaces, the district also hosts the headquarters of the Saudi stock exchange along with multinationals such as Goldman Sachs.

The Houthis have stepped up their attacks against Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, striking military, civilian and oil infrastructure.

The major attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport forced the suspension of flights for two weeks. Several events have been cancelled, including the Future Investment Initiative financial conference, dubbed “Davos in the desert”.

In response, a Saudi-led military coalition fighting on behalf of Yemen’s government has been striking Houthi targets in the impoverished country.

On Tuesday, local officials said a coalition air strike on buses and trucks killed 26 people in Lahj province. Government forces blamed the Houthis for the attack.

As the conflict shows no sign of slowing, Britain sanctioned the Houthis and four of its top officials “for deliberately attempting to undermine stability” on Tuesday.

The measures include an asset freeze against the group and an asset freeze and travel ban on four figures, including security and intelligence head Abdul Hakim Hashem Ali al-Khaiwani, and interior affairs official Abdulkarim Amir al-Din Hussein al-Houthi.

The Saudi-led coalition intervened in Yemen in early 2015, after the Houthis had captured the capital Sanaa and sent the internationally recognised government fleeing to Aden.

The war left hundreds of thousands dead and triggered a humanitarian catastrophe before an uneasy ceasefire went into effect in 2022.

sources.headline: Houthis hit Riyadh's tallest tower, 11 wounded, Saudi Civil defense says
sources.text: Nov 24 - Yemen's Houthi fighters struck the tallest tower in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, on Tuesday for the second time in less than a week, wounding at least 11 people as the group presses on with a campaign that has disrupted the Gulf's biggest economy.Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense reported the injuries and posted a picture of the landmark tower housing the headquarters of the Saudi Public Investment Fund.The image showed some damage to the building about halfway up the facade, similar to the impact from a strike on the same tower on November 19, which caused damage but no injuries. Reuters could not immediately determine when the image was taken or the extent of the further damage from the latest strike.The Saudi-led coalition fighting against Yemen's Houthis said later on Tuesday that the attack was carried out with a drone, adding that it would respond "decisively to the deliberate targeting of civilians and civilian property" by Houthis.The Houthi militia, which controls much of western Yemen including the capital Sanaa, has been firing at Saudi airports, oil infrastructure and office buildings since Yemen's frozen civil war reignited in July in a knock-on from the US-Iran war.The attacks have caused the cancellation of most international flights to Riyadh, and forced Saudi Arabia to postpone or cancel major international events, including soccer's AFC Asian Cup.On the ground in Yemen, the war has caused a major humanitarian crisis, with hundreds of thousands of people displaced from their homes since July.The Houthis have seized swathes of territory, forcing forces aligned with the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government to stage a major retreat this month. The Saudi-led coalition has conducted widespread air strikes. REUTERS
